source_title: Extended Follow-Up and Spatial Analysis of the American Cancer Society Study Linking Particulate Air Pollution and Mortality (HEI Research Report 140)
evidence: Table 3 ('HRs of Pollutants and Ecologic Risk Factors for Selected Causes of Death from the Standard Cox Model'), PDF page 29 (printed page 19). PM2.5 (1979-1983 monitoring period, 58 MSAs, n=351,338), All Causes, standard Cox model with no ecologic-covariate adjustment: HR=1.06 (95% CI 1.04-1.08) per 10 ug/m3 increment. This is the primary all-cause coefficient Huang & Peng (2025) cite as 'the estimate from the American Cancer Society' (their Table 3, ref 45; see huang_peng_2025_eq2_4). beta = ln(HR)/increment = ln(1.06)/10 = 0.0058269 per ug/m3; ci_low = ln(1.04)/10 = 0.0039221; ci_high = ln(1.08)/10 = 0.0076961. This matches the task brief's expectation of HR near 1.06 per 10 ug/m3 / beta approx 0.0058, so no material discrepancy to flag.

source_title: Extended Follow-Up and Spatial Analysis of the American Cancer Society Study Linking Particulate Air Pollution and Mortality (HEI Research Report 140)
evidence: Table 1 ('Distribution of Air Pollutants at the Individual Level'), PDF page 28 (printed page 18). PM2.5 (1979-1983), n=58 MSAs / 351,338 participants: mean 21.20 ug/m3, variance 21.40, percentiles 0/5/10/25/50/75/90/95/100 = 10.77 / 13.73 / 14.91 / 17.85 / 21.69 / 24.12 / 26.75 / 27.89 / 30.01 ug/m3. The 0th percentile (10.77 ug/m3) is the lowest individual-level PM2.5 concentration measured in the same 1979-1983 exposure metric that produced the Table 3 all-cause HR=1.06 used for beta (krewski_2009_table3_hr), so it is the natural lower bound of the exposure range the coefficient was actually estimated over.

source_title: Substantial air quality and health co-benefits from combined federal and subnational climate actions in the United States. One Earth 8, 101232.
evidence: Equations 2-4 and surrounding 'Health-impact assessment' text, PDF page 16. Confirms AF = 1 - exp(-beta*DeltaPM) (attributable fraction) and DeltaY = AF x Y0 x Pop (Equation 2), and that mortality in a given year is summed over county c and age group a (Equations 3-4). States: 'Our main results use the following Krewski et al. log-linear health-impact function from BenMAP... here we use the estimate from the American Cancer Society; we use the same estimate each year from 2015 to 2030.' Also states GEMM is used only 'as a sensitivity analysis' and that GEMM-based deaths are 'around 200% higher' -- confirms GEMM is a distinct, secondary CRF appropriately deferred out of this task's scope rather than implemented or stubbed.

source_title: Substantial air quality and health co-benefits from combined federal and subnational climate actions in the United States. One Earth 8, 101232.
evidence: Equations 5-7 and the 'Decomposition analysis' subsection, PDF page 16. As transcribed, Equation 5 (A = 2015Mortality x [2030 Pop_c,a / 2015 Pop_c,a]) subscripts the population ratio by district c and age band a. Applied literally, that ratio already carries the future age structure into A, which would force B-A (the paper's stated 'population aging effect') to be identically zero -- not a meaningful decomposition term. This task's implementation instead scales 2015 Mortality by the AGGREGATE population ratio (sum of Pop over all c,a in 2030, divided by the same sum in 2015) to build A, holding age composition, Y0, and AF fixed at 2015 values; B then substitutes in the true 2030 age-specific population by (c,a), so B-A isolates the aging effect. This is a documented interpretive reading of an ambiguous equation, not a verbatim transcription -- see docs/methods/health_impact_assessment.md and the task summary.

source_title: HIA South Korea: Time for a Check Up
evidence: 'Health Impact Assessment & Economic Valuation' section, PDF page 25 of the report as fetched and re-paginated for this task (front matter/pagination may differ from the publisher's own page numbers). States the methodology is 'adapted from CREA's Quantifying the Economic Costs of Air Pollution from Fossil Fuels (Myllyvirta 2020)' and that 'Data on total population and population age structure, as well as all mortality results, baseline death rates and years of life lost for South Korea were taken from the GBD project 2019 (IHME 2020). The baseline concentrations of PM2.5 and NO2 were taken from van Donkelaar et al. (2016) and Larkin et al. (2017), respectively.' No explicit numeric counterfactual, TMREL, or threshold concentration for the PM2.5-mortality function is stated anywhere in the report text; it relies on GBD 2019's integrated exposure-response (IER) function, which has its own built-in TMREL not disclosed in this document and a non-log-linear functional form, unlike the Krewski log-linear CRF implemented in this task. Establishes Korean HIA precedent for a GBD-based approach, but supplies no numeric value usable as our counterfactual_ugm3.

source_title: Long-Term Exposure to Particulate Matter and Mortality: An Update of the WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Int J Public Health 69:1607683.
evidence: Searched throughout (PDF pages 1-13) for an explicit counterfactual, TMREL, or 'below which no effect' threshold value. The paper reports narrative findings that several individual cohorts (e.g. CanCHEC, discussed pp.7-9) found 'no evidence for a threshold below which no [association]' and gives a pooled all-cause RR=1.095 (95% CI 1.064-1.127) per 10 ug/m3 (matching the figure already recorded in docs/references/literature/README.md), but does not itself state a numeric WHO Air Quality Guideline annual value or a TMREL. It is the supporting systematic review commissioned for the 2021 WHO AQG development, not the AQG guideline document itself (which is not held in this repository). Not usable as a sourced counterfactual number without acquiring the actual WHO AQG 2021 guideline document and adding it to docs/references/literature/.
